title: Witnesses to the Ends of the Earth
summary: Luke opens his second volume by recalling Jesus' forty days of appearances after the resurrection and his command to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit. Jesus promises power for witness from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth and is taken up into heaven, with the promise that he will return. The apostles pray with the women, Mary, and Jesus' brothers, and choose Matthias by lot to take the place of Judas.
story: The Gospel of Luke ended with the risen Jesus blessing his disciples near Bethany and being carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50-53). Acts retells that ending in more detail and turns it into a beginning. The disciples still expect a political restoration of Israel's kingdom; Jesus redirects them to a wider and different task. Verse 8 sets out the plan of the whole book: witness in Jerusalem (chapters 1 to 7), in Judea and Samaria (chapters 8 to 12), and to the ends of the earth (chapters 13 to 28). Before the Spirit comes, the community waits, prays, and restores the number of the Twelve, preparing for the Pentecost of chapter 2.
historical:
The events follow the resurrection, around AD 30 or 33, and lead up to the Jewish feast of Pentecost fifty days after Passover. The forty days of appearances fill the time between Easter and the ascension. Jerusalem was under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, and the temple was run by the high priest Caiaphas and the leading priestly families, the same men who had handed Jesus over weeks before. That the apostles gathered openly in the city at all is worth noticing.

The Mount of Olives rises just east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley. A Sabbath day's travel was the distance Jewish custom allowed on the Sabbath, about two thousand cubits, a little over half a mile, based on rabbinic reading of passages like Exodus 16:29 and Joshua 3:4. Luke's note simply tells his readers the mountain was close. The list of the apostles matches Luke 6:14-16 minus Judas Iscariot. Simon is called the Zealot, which may mean he had belonged to a movement zealous for the law and hostile to Rome, or may simply describe his zeal; the organized Zealot party is attested by the Jewish historian Josephus mainly for the war of AD 66 to 70.
cultural:
Theophilus, the man addressed in verse 1 as in Luke 1:3, was probably a real patron, perhaps of some standing, since Luke calls him most excellent in the Gospel. His name means friend of God or loved by God, and some have taken it as symbolic, though a real person is more likely. Ancient historians often opened a second volume by summarizing the first, as Luke does here.

Casting lots was a common way in Israel to leave a decision to God. Priests divided their duties by lot (Luke 1:9), land was divided by lot in Joshua, and Proverbs 16:33 says that the lot is cast into the lap but its every decision is from the LORD. The apostles first narrow the choice by clear qualifications, then pray, then cast lots. Notably, this is the last time lots are used for such a decision in the New Testament; after Pentecost the church seeks guidance through the Spirit, prayer, and counsel. The upper room was probably a large room on the roof level of a house, a common place for gatherings.
literary: Acts 1 is a bridge. Verses 1 to 11 overlap with the end of Luke, and verses 12 to 26 set the stage for Pentecost. Luke uses a prologue (1-2), a summary (3), a dialogue (4-8), a scene of departure with angelic interpreters (9-11), a list (13), and a speech by Peter (16-22), the first of many speeches in the book. The parenthesis in verses 18-19, explaining Judas's death to readers who would not know Aramaic, shows Luke writing for a Greek-speaking audience. Key words that will run through Acts appear here first: the Spirit, power, witness, kingdom, and Jerusalem.

outline.t: Wait for the Spirit; you will be My witnesses
The ascension and the promise of return
Peter explains the need to replace Judas

doctrines.note: Jesus calls the Spirit the gift the Father promised and says the disciples will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, drawing on John the Baptist's words (Luke 3:16). The Spirit's coming is tied to power for witness. The book will show what that means.

Verse 8 is not only a command but a promise: you will be My witnesses. The mission moves outward geographically and crosses ethnic and religious lines, from Jews in Jerusalem to Samaritans to the Gentile world.

Jesus spent the forty days speaking about the kingdom of God. The disciples ask if he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He does not deny that God has plans for Israel, but he refuses to give a timetable and turns them to witness as the way the kingdom now advances.
The angels promise that “This same Jesus” will come back in the same way he went. The ascension does not mean Jesus is absent or finished; it means he reigns and will return in person.

words.note: Martus, witness. A witness in the ancient world was someone who testified to what he had seen or heard, often in a legal setting. The apostles' first qualification is that they have seen the risen Jesus (1:22). Because so many witnesses paid with their lives, the word later came to mean martyr, but here it means one who testifies.

Dunamis, power or ability. The power Jesus promises is not political power (the disciples were thinking of a restored kingdom) but the Spirit's enabling for witness. The English word dynamite comes from it, but that tells us nothing about its meaning in the first century; the point is the ability God gives to do what the disciples could not do alone.

Analambano, to take up. Luke uses it for the ascension in verses 2, 11, and 22. The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for Elijah being taken up into heaven (2 Kings 2:11), and there are further echoes: Elijah's successor received a double portion of his spirit after seeing him taken up, and here the disciples who see Jesus go will receive his Spirit.

Kleros, lot, and by extension a share or portion assigned. In verse 17 Peter says Judas had a share in this ministry (the same word), and in verse 26 the lot falls to Matthias. The word links the method of choosing with the portion received: apostleship is a share given by God, not a position seized.

christ: Acts 1 shows the risen Jesus alive, teaching, and then exalted to heaven. His ascension is not an escape but an enthronement: from the Father's right hand he will pour out the Spirit (2:33) and direct his church. Luke's first sentence implies that his Gospel told what Jesus began to do and to teach, so that Acts will tell what he continues to do. The cloud that hides him recalls the cloud of God's presence in Israel's history and Daniel's vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). The angels' promise of his return in the same way anchors Christian hope in a personal, visible coming of the same Jesus.

hard.q: Matthew says Judas hanged himself, but Acts says he fell headlong and burst open. Do the accounts contradict each other?
hard.a:
Matthew 27:3-10 says Judas threw the silver into the temple and hanged himself, and the priests used the money to buy a potter's field for burying strangers, called the Field of Blood. Acts says Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, fell headlong, and burst open, and the field was called Akeldama, Field of Blood.

Since early times readers have offered harmonizations: Judas hanged himself, and the body later fell (perhaps when the rope or branch gave way) and burst; and the field was bought with his money by the priests, so that it could be said he acquired it. Others think the two accounts preserve independent traditions about Judas's death that agree on the essentials (a shameful death, a field bought with his blood money and named Field of Blood) but differ in detail, and they do not think harmonizing is necessary. Either way, both writers present his end as the tragic outcome of betrayal and as fulfilling Scripture.

questions: The disciples asked about times and seasons, and Jesus gave them a task instead. What questions about the future tend to distract you from what you have been given to do now?
The first thing the community did after the ascension was pray together. What would it look like for your church or group to wait and pray before acting?
Jesus said you will be My witnesses. Who is your Jerusalem, your Judea and Samaria, and your ends of the earth?
